posts.author: LarryD
posts.content_md: Is there a limit to the number of holograms we can enter in the contest?

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
I see nothing wrong with multiple entries. Each entry will be judged solely on it's own merits anyway. After all, the point of this excercise is promote making holograms, so the more you make the better!

Opinions?

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** I see nothing wrong with multiple entries. Each entry will be judged solely on it's own merits anyway. After all, the point of this excercise is promote making holograms, so the more you make the better!Opinions?

I would tend to agree, but I see a potential problem with vote-splitting. For example, if A submits 2 holos gaining vote percentages of 33% and 33% each while B submits 1 holo with a vote percentage of 34%. I would have to say that the hologram submitted by B should win, even though A got lots more total votes and would likely have won by submitting only 1 hologram. But it is a contest for best hologram, not best holographer.

While I can imagine that a runoff or proportional voting scheme might remedy this somewhat, it starts getting awfully complicated. I think it would simplest to permit multiple entries, but to point out that that this is a non-optimal strategy if winning is the objective. The rational thing to do would be to make one official entry and to display any other work in the regular gallery. The expectation would be that the voters would consider all work submitted when choosing which official entry to vote for.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:c64e45118f="TomB"]The rational thing to do would be to make one official entry and to display any other work in the regular gallery. The expectation would be that the voters would consider all work submitted when choosing which official entry to vote for.[/quote:c64e45118f]

How does one look for other work in the gallery? Presumably, in your scheme, any entrant who does have other work(s) posted in the gallery (or elsewhere?) should have a link to them. Personally, I think that while ideally other work should be taken into consideration, that'd be counter-productive to the intent. The idea is to promote the shooting of holograms and so to produce a new work for the contest and the contest should be about the best hologram (taking into account more than just technical excellence). If multiple entries come in that are created for the contest, they should be allowed into the contest. Otherwise you could simply make a god-awful hologram and point to your winning entry last time and probably win again

posts.content_md:
> **LarryD:** So the basis of the contest is all about the best holo, not best holographer, and each entry stands on it's own, right

Yes, ideally. The contest premise (judging holograms of catlike objects by their 2D images) is intentionally absurd, but if it gets people motivated to make and show their holograms (well, at least 2D images of them), it's worthwhile. 

One interesting method of ranking images is by showing randomly selected pairs to many viewers, asking them to choose between the two. A nifty example of this is [http://www.kittenwar.com](http://www.kittenwar.com)

An interesting problem in statistics! What would be the chance of any particular entry winning if you pursued a method of showing two random ones at a time, eliminating the losing one, adding the winning one to the pool and repeating till you found a winner rather than simply showing them all at once.

I think it's more of a problem in human psychology, i.e. the relationship between pairwise ranking and global ranking. I seem to recall that it's been shown that humans are very illogical about such things.

If picture ranks were objectively determinable, the kittenwar method would eventually produce the same result as the the global method, just much more slowly - they are just different sorting methods, with kittenwar being similar to a bubble sort algorithm.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:c0ff94b243="DJ Mathson"]Please Dinesh, show us the statistics. I for one want to see the answer. [/quote:c0ff94b243]

Well, if you insist 

Bear in mind, statistics was never my favourite subject. I, sort of, believe:"There are lies, there are damned lies and there are statistics". However, let's proceed in this way. You have a bin of all the entries (let's call it bin_1 and N entries), you take two out and pick one, either by merit or by chance. The losing entry is discarded and the winning entry goes into another bin(bin_2). You conitinue this until there are none in bin_1, ie there were an even number of entries, or there is one, ie there was an odd number. If there is 1 left over, you transfer that into bin_2 unjudged. You repeat the process with a new bin, bin_3. You n=continue this process till there is only one left in bin_n.

The number os ways to pick 2 objects out of N is 2_C_N, where

n_C_r = n!/(r!)((r-n)!)

Thus, having picked two objects, there are now N-2 left in bin_1. Repeat to give 2_C_(N-2), 2_C_N-4...2_N_N-m, where m N-m=0 so that we have the number of ways, W_1, of picking all the entries to place in bin_2 is:

W_1 = 2_C_N + 2_C_N-2 + 2_C_N-4 + ...+2_C_N-m.

If each pair is chsen at random, then there is a probability of 0.5 of picking either of the pair. So, the probability of your hologram being transferred from bin1 to bin_2, P_1 is:

P_1 = 0.5*W_1

If the entries are chosen by merit, then we'd have to introduce an "expectation value" of probabilities of characteristics N_1 (which may represent, say, beauty), N_2 (which may represent technical ability) etc. In this case:

P_1 = (0.5)(N_! + N_2 +...N_q)*(W_1)

We can then proceed in this way to get the appropriate probabilities of surviving into bin_3, bin_4 etc. Finally, the final probablitiy that yours will win is using the "bin" method:

P_bin = 1/( P_1*P_2*P_3....)

However, if they're all presented all at once,P_all,, then the only method I can see is an "expectation value" method, but altered to the fact that the "result of experiment" is the number of judges, J_n, in each of n categories:

P_all = N_1*J_1 + N_2*J_2 + ...N_m*J_m

It seems off hand, that the number of entries and the number of judgement criteria will determine which of these two methods will succesfully get a "win". Since the ratio of P_bin/P_all depends on the number of terms in each case.

This is a (very!) back-of-an-envelope calculation, so it's probably nowhere near as rigorous as it should be. In other words, take it with a large dose of salts!

[quote:c0ff94b243="TomB"]If picture ranks were objectively determinable, the kittenwar method would eventually produce the same result as the the global method, just much more slowly - they are just different sorting methods, with kittenwar being similar to a bubble sort algorithm.[/quote:c0ff94b243]

I'd think it'd be a buuble sort algorithm if you were ranking. If you were simply picking "the best hologram", wouldn't it be a matter of elimination, rather than one of sorting?

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** I'd think it'd be a buuble sort algorithm if you were ranking. If you were simply picking "the best hologram", wouldn't it be a matter of elimination, rather than one of sorting?

Good point. I was thinking of the kittenwar scheme as working like a uncoordinated parallel distributed bubble sort. If there was only one judge, it would just be a matter of picking the best, requiring ony N-1 binary comparisons. With M judges, I suppose they could each pick their favorite, but then it's hard to see how the results could be fairly merged without having retained relative rank information or scores which would make the process much less efficient...

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
I agree, with M judges you'd have to have some form of ranking, which means each judge has the pool, ranks them and passes them on to the next judge. The next judge does not have the first judges's ranking, but ranks them independantly. You'd then have to have some scheme to eliminate the lower ranks and repeat the process. Finally you'd have a winner. Joy has been trying to explain something they do in baseball called "round robin". Unfortunately, she's none too clear on the concept either.

One other way is to do what they do at the Olympics. Each entry gets a score, or possible more than one based on some characteristic such as technical ability, imagination etc. Each category is then judged "the best" in that particular category. Of course, this means multiple prizes - one for each category - or some way of choosing "the best" by melding the categories. I must say, I prefer the "give each entry a score" approach, which then implies a straight ranking.
